questions.q: Name the protein subunit that polymerizes into the microtubule triplets of a centriole and state the exact arrangement (number of triplets and their angular spacing) in a mature centriole.
questions.a: The subunit is α/β-tubulin heterodimer; a mature centriole has nine microtubule triplets arranged at 40° intervals around a central cartwheel hub. A wrong answer (e.g., "actin filaments" or "9 doublets") reveals confusion between centriole (9×3) and axoneme (9+2) architecture, or between cytoskeletal systems.

questions.q: A student claims: "Plant cells lack centrosomes because they have a cell wall that prevents spindle formation." Explain why this statement is incorrect by identifying the actual microtubule-organizing centres in higher plants and describing how spindle assembly occurs without centrioles.
questions.a: Higher plants lack centrioles but possess acentriolar microtubule-organizing centres (MTOCs) at the nuclear envelope and cortical microtubule arrays; spindle microtubules nucleate from these dispersed MTOCs and self-organize into a bipolar spindle via motor proteins (kinesin-5, dynein). The cell wall does not impede spindle formation — it only fixes cell geometry. A wrong answer indicates the misconception that centrosome = spindle, ignoring alternative nucleation pathways.

questions.q: In a hypotonic medium, a *Chlamydomonas* cell (with a contractile vacuole) and a mature plant mesophyll cell (with a large central vacuole) both experience water influx. Predict which cell will swell and burst first if the contractile vacuole is chemically inhibited, and justify using tonoplast transport energetics.
questions.a: The *Chlamydomonas* cell will burst first. Its contractile vacuole actively expels water using ATP-driven proton pumps (V-ATPase) that create an electrochemical gradient for ion/water efflux; inhibition stops this active osmoregulation. The plant cell's central vacuole accumulates solutes via tonoplast H⁺-pyrophosphatase and antiporters, generating high turgor that is mechanically resisted by the rigid cell wall — no active water expulsion needed. Wrong prediction reveals misunderstanding of active vs. passive osmotic management.

questions.q: Compare the biogenesis of a centriole (procentriole assembly) with the formation of a plant central vacuole from provacuoles. Identify two shared molecular principles and one fundamental difference in membrane involvement.
questions.a: Shared: (1) both require templated assembly — SAS-6 cartwheel for centriole, SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion for vacuole; (2) both depend on cell-cycle-regulated kinase activity (PLK4 for centriole, CDKA for vacuole biogenesis). Difference: centriole assembly is non-membranous (proteinaceous scaffold in cytoplasm), whereas vacuole formation is entirely membrane-driven (ER/Golgi-derived vesicles coalesce into a tonoplast-bound compartment). Confusing the two as "both membranous" or "both protein-only" shows failure to distinguish organellar biogenesis modes.

questions.q: A research paper reports that RNAi knockdown of *SPAS-1* (a pericentriolar protein) in *C. elegans* causes monopolar spindles but normal cilia. Evaluate whether this result supports or contradicts the dual-function model of centrosomes (spindle + basal body). Propose a mechanistic explanation.
questions.a: The result *supports* functional modularity: SPAS-1 is specifically required for pericentriolar material (PCM) recruitment of γ-tubulin ring complexes (γ-TuRCs) for spindle nucleation, but dispensable for centriole-to-basal-body conversion and transition zone assembly that template cilia. This shows the same centriole cylinder can independently nucleate distinct microtubule arrays via separable protein modules. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "contradicts because centrosome does both") misses the concept of modular PCM composition.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using *Rhoeo* leaf epidermal peels and solutions of varying solute concentrations to demonstrate tonoplast selectivity. Specify the observable parameter, control, and how you would distinguish tonoplast-mediated ion accumulation from passive diffusion.
questions.a: Incubate peels in 0.3 M mannitol (isotonic) vs. 0.3 M NaCl + fluorescent dye (e.g., BCECF for pH, or radiolabeled ²²Na⁺). Observable: vacuolar sap concentration (via plasmolysis gradient or fluorescence ratio). Control: heat-killed peels (denatured transporters). Active accumulation shows higher vacuolar [Na⁺] or lower pH than external medium despite isotonic mannitol; passive diffusion equilibrates. Poor design omits killed control or uses only plasmolysis (which reflects water potential, not ion selectivity).
